p: On a January drill weekend a pilot vacancy went up on the corkboard in Kit's shop. The board sits Saturday, July 10, and Kit turns thirty three on June 3, which by the posting's age line puts her five weeks over.
When Boyd asked if she was thinking about it, she said yes, and that he'd hear it from her first. He said that seven years ago he'd asked her to stay.
Page two of the posting says an application starts with the applicant's immediate supervisor. For Kit, that's Boyd.
In the break room Kemp told everyone the colonel had sent an avionics tech named Corbin Haas to pilot training two years ago, and he washed out.
At the Riverside Diner Kit met Vern Pruett, who navigated two two eight for twenty one years. She asked him to teach her for the test, and he told her Tuesday at seven, at his house on Cedar Street.
At home she told Graham she wanted it. His okay came a beat late.
Corbin Haas. Technical sergeant in the avionics shop. Two years ago the wing sent him to pilot training, and he washed out.
Joanna Merritt. Colonel and wing commander. She flies the KC-135 herself, and the wing's pick for the pilot slot goes through her.
On Monday morning Kit came off a night shift at the water plant at seven, drove the river road to the base with the heater on high, and walked into the shop still smelling faintly of chlorine.

The routing slip had come off the wing's email Sunday night. One page, stapled to the front of her application, with five signature blocks down the right side. The top one said IMMEDIATE SUPERVISOR. She'd filled in everything else at the break table at the plant, at two in the morning between feed checks, and then sat looking at that empty block for a long time, as if it might sign itself.

Boyd worked on base full time, so on weekdays the shop was his. His office was the one by the tool crib, with a door he never closed and a photo on the wall from 1996: two two eight on a gray morning, and Boyd in front of the nose gear at twenty, skinny as a safety wire.
She put the package on his desk. That's the pilot package. You're the first block.
Boyd read the top page. He read the second. Then he set the whole thing in his inbox, on top of a parts request, and put his coffee cup on the corner of it.

She waited for him to look up. He didn't. On the drive home she counted the weeks to June 1, when her scores had to be on file, and got a little over twenty, and after that she couldn't stop counting.

Tuesday, January 12, at seven o'clock, Kit parked on Cedar Street in front of a brick ranch with a hedge out front that had been dead so long it had gone silver. Nineteen hundred, he'd said at the diner. She was four minutes early and sat in the truck for three of them.

Vern opened the door before she knocked. The kitchen had a yellow table, a percolator, and a coffee can full of pencils somebody had sharpened with a knife. Through the doorway she could see the den: a long slanted table under a lamp, the kind navigators plotted on, and a banker's box on the end of it with 2001 written on the side in marker. She'd been seven that summer. She looked at the box a beat too long, and then she didn't ask, the same as at the diner. Somewhere down the hall a television was on low.
Sit. He tore a sheet off a legal pad, printed one word on it in his square capitals, and turned it around. CIRCUMSPECT.
You get twelve seconds a word on this one. Most words you'll know or you won't. This one, don't guess. Take it apart. What's it mean?

Careful. Circum is around and spect is look. You look all the way around before you do anything. Vern tapped the pad with his pencil. Most people get the look and stop there. The word's about what you do after. He took the pad back. More capitals.
Vern set the pad aside and dug an index card out of his shirt pocket, already written, the corner rounded off from riding there. CONTENT IS TO ELATED AS ANNOYED IS TO BLANK.

Not content like the stuff in a box. Content like a navigator with a fix that'll do. Elated is three stars crossing in one tidy point on the chart, which happened to me maybe four times in twenty years. He pushed the card at her. Make your sentence.

Elated is way more content. Furious is way more annoyed. She could hear the sentence take the weight of both pairs. Vern put the card back in his shirt pocket and buttoned the flap. Degree. Same feeling, more of it.

At twenty to eight Vern got the egg timer out of the drawer by the stove. It was white plastic, with a crack down one side that somebody had glued. He cranked it to eight. Then he dealt twenty five index cards onto the table the way you'd deal gin rummy. Analogies, one to a card, in his capitals.
Eight minutes. Same as the real one. Go.

She went. Card one was a chisel. She fought it. The second she turned over twice. By the time she thought to check the egg it had ticked down to three, with ten cards face down by her elbow and fifteen still waiting.
Vern hadn't moved. Fifteen to go, three minutes on the egg. What does each one get now?

Twelve. A hundred and eighty seconds, fifteen cards. Vern asked what the first ten had cost her, and she told him thirty apiece. He grunted. The egg kept going. She ran the last fifteen at twelve seconds a card, missed three, and would have missed those three with a week to think.
The egg went off. Vern pushed his chair back, went into the den, and came back with one sheet out of the banker's box. Not the box. He laid it on the table facing her.

My log, sixteen January, oh one. Tolliver to the track and home, six point one hours. Celestial check at oh four ten Zulu. Stars scintillating bad below twenty degrees, so I shot the high ones. Lieutenant Merritt, copilot, first track with us. She asked what scintillate means. Told her twinkle. Looked it up at the table in my pocket dictionary. From scintilla, a spark.
Kit read the name twice. She'd only ever seen it typed, at the bottom of wing emails about parking and the holiday party. The colonel?

She was a lieutenant once. Everybody was. Far as this table goes, she's still the Lieutenant. He tapped the last line. The eraser on his pencil was worn down to the metal. One a week. You don't get the box. Now. Scintilla's a spark. A man tells you there isn't a scintilla of doubt. How much doubt is there?

None. Not even a spark's worth. Vern creased the log down the middle with his thumbnail and handed it across. Next Tuesday, three words with the same front end as circumspect. Out of your head. Not out of a book. She put the log in her coat with the diner napkin.
Ten days later the slip was still in Boyd's inbox. She'd had two Tuesdays at the yellow table by then, and two logs in her coat.

Thursday, January 21, she had a day off from the plant and drove out to the base for no reason she'd have admitted to anybody. Midweek the shop ran on four people and a radio. She walked past his office to the coffee pot, and there it was, under the same cup, with a second coffee ring on it now beside the first. The top block was empty. She'd told him he'd hear it from her first, and he had. He'd heard it and put a cup on it.

Down the hall the first sergeant's door stood open, with a bowl of peppermints on the desk, there for exactly the kind of airman who had a problem with her supervisor. Across the street, in the headquarters building with the flags out front, the colonel's exec kept her calendar on a very clean desk. Kit thought about both of them before she'd finished pouring.
Boyd was on the phone in his office with the door open, arguing with somebody about a parts delivery.

She waited out the call, all of it, including the part where he spelled his own name twice for the parts guy. Then she stepped in and shut the door. Boyd looked at the door before he looked at her. Is it the slip, or is it me? Boyd studied the coffee ring as if it were a leak he had to trace. It isn't you. Then what is it? It's a lot of names after mine, Sergeant. He slid the cup off the corner and onto the parts request. He didn't pick the slip up. Give me till drill. Okay. She did mean it. He could see that, and it seemed to make it worse for him.

Leadership and Communication. His block's the top one, so his is the first conversation, and you had it with the door shut instead of across a coffee pot. You asked what was wrong instead of telling him what he owed you. Did he sign? No. A direct try doesn't promise a yes. It earns you the next step if you need one, and you haven't needed one yet.

The avionics back shop smelled like solder and hot dust. Corbin Haas was at the far bench with an airspeed indicator clamped in a fixture and two hoses running from it to a test set, watching the needle climb.
He was thirty four, a technical sergeant, and two years ago the wing had sent him to pilot training. That part everybody knew.
Darrow, he said to the needle. Kemp showed up Monday with a donut and an apology. Took him a while to say whose idea it was. I figure I owe you half the donut. Word on the ramp is you put in for it.
It's in Boyd's inbox. Under a coffee cup.

Mine sat under a stapler for a month. He nodded at the shelf over the bench, where three instruments sat in a row with yellow repair tags hanging off them: an airspeed indicator, an altimeter, a vertical speed indicator. Since they're going to ask you anyway. Pitot side, static side. Which of those three needs both?

Airspeed. Ram air up the pitot tube, quiet air off the static port, and the needle's the difference. Corbin let go of the knob on the test set. Ice up the pitot and you've got one liar on the panel. Which one? You just told me which one.
He shut the test set off. For a while he just coiled the hose.

Everybody wants to know what happened. Nobody asks. They ask Kemp. He hung the hose over a nail. I was good on paper. Good in the books. Then they strap you in with an instructor behind you who writes down every single thing your hands do, and pretty soon you're flying his clipboard instead of the airplane.
He worked a rag over his knuckles, one at a time.
I gave the bars back. Shop took me home.
Kemp had told that story a dozen ways in the break room. None of them had the bars in it.
He looked at her then, straight on, the way he'd check a torque stripe. So what happens to you if you wash out? Somebody ought to ask you that before the board does.

I come home and crew a jet. Same as you. She hadn't known that was the answer until it was out. What would you do different? Corbin took his time with it. I'd have told somebody the truth sooner. I told everybody it was going fine, right up to the day it wasn't. He picked up the next indicator. Doesn't help you with the test. It didn't. It helped with something else, and she drove home with it.

He asked what everybody else was too polite to. You answered it plainly, then asked what he knows. Mentoring runs uphill sometimes, and nobody else in this wing has been where you're headed. On the test that's how you treat someone with experience you don't have: answer straight, ask, then listen. He gave you more than a test tip, didn't he?
On Friday, February 5, the fridge whiteboard slid off its bracket and down the door with the whole week still on it. Kit went out to the garage for the drill.

The garage was cold enough to see her breath. The drill hung on the pegboard and its battery didn't. She looked on the workbench, then behind the mower, where things went to be forgotten. Back against the wall there was a blue tarp over something with corners, about as tall as her hip. Graham's, she figured. A school thing. She found the battery in a jar of screws on the shelf and went back in.

Graham already had the whiteboard back up, with a butter knife. The drill sat on the counter, unneeded. He was at the table with a stack of index cards held together by a rubber band, made on his lunch period in the printing he used on lab quizzes. A hundred of them, he said. Words on the front, meanings on the back, and some analogies he'd written himself.
When do you book the test?

After the slip, then. He said it the way he wrote on the whiteboard, one more block in the week. She heard it go up next to the degree and the inspection, and she let it stay there. Then he turned over the first card. INSULATOR CURRENT. Pick the pair that matches. I'll read you four.
An insulator stops current. A dam stops a river. Graham turned the card over to check his own answer, which made her laugh. Sorry. Habit.

An insulator blocks the flow of current. A dam blocks the flow of a river. One sentence, both pairs. The pick a pair items are the same skill run backward: build the sentence from the stem, then push each pair through it. The pair that fits the sentence tightest wins.

Saturday was drill. At 5:40 in the morning Kit and Fisk sat in the crew truck with the heater roaring, waiting on the forms. Fisk still had the warehouse scanner on its lanyard, bumping his chest every time he shifted. Kemp's two airmen were in the back seat with their hoods up, faking sleep about as well as anybody does at that hour.
Fisk had been quiet since the gate. Then he said it to the windshield. Kemp says you're going to be a pilot.
She let the wipers go across twice before she said anything, and he turned in his seat. So who gets two two eight?

Come help me with the chocks. Out by the nose wheel the wind came straight off the river and took every word sideways. I put in for it. Odds are lousy and it's months out. If it happens, I want her going to you. Fisk looked at the jet as if he'd never seen it before. Me? Who else knows where my flashlight is? That got a laugh out of him, a short one that fogged in front of his face. So we start on the things I don't write down.

Mentoring and Communication. He asked about his own future, so he gets a straight answer, away from people who'd turn it into a story. You told him what you knew and what you didn't, and then you handed him a job. He can put weight on that, even if this whole thing falls through. Was any of it a promise you can't keep? No.

By ten the wind had swung around out of the northwest. The thermometer screwed to the hangar door said 10, and nobody believed it was that warm. Boyd had put tire servicing on two two eight on the morning board, so it was going to be Kit and Fisk kneeling on frozen concrete by the main gear for an hour, maybe longer.

Every truck had the shop's cold weather card taped to the dash, curling at one corner from the defroster. Wind chill chart on top: wind speed in miles an hour along the top edge, air temperature down the left, a wind chill in each box. Under it, the shop's warm up rule, printed on label maker tape.

The cold weather card off the dash. Wind speed runs along the top, air temperature down the left side, and each box holds the wind chill. Underneath, the shop's warm up rule. Above minus five, every hour. Minus five to minus fourteen, every thirty minutes. Minus fifteen or colder, every fifteen.
The flag by base ops was standing straight out, and the weather on her phone said wind fifteen.

Finger on the 10 row, finger on the 15 column, slide. Minus 7. She checked next door both ways, minus 4 and minus 9, so she'd know what a slip would look like. Thirty minutes on, then the truck. I'll keep the clock. I'm fine, Sergeant. You've been up since yesterday. Thirty minutes.

Ten degrees is a row. Fifteen miles an hour is a column. The answer lives where they cross, and the cells around it are the traps: minus 4 to the left, minus 9 to the right, 0 above, minus 13 below. Table Reading builds many of its wrong answers out of the neighbors. Anchor both headings before you read a number.
At two that afternoon the wing commander came down the line on foot, one jet at a time, with a cup of coffee and nobody trailing her.

Colonel Joanna Merritt was forty nine and still flew the KC-135 herself a few times a month. She stopped under the pilot's window of two two eight and read the stencil, CREW CHIEF SSGT K. DARROW, as if she were reading a roster.
It took Kit a second to match her to a line of block capitals on Vern's log. LT MERRITT, COPILOT, FIRST TRACK WITH US.
Sergeant Darrow. I hear you're interested in my pilot slot. Nothing's come across my desk. Where is it?
It's with my flight chief, ma'am. It'll come to you through him. Merritt didn't say anything for a moment. Good. That's where it belongs.
Merritt didn't move on. She turned the cup a quarter turn in her hand.
Tell me why. Not why you deserve it.

Kit had an answer. She'd put it together at the corkboard in January and been sanding on it ever since. The wing's going to need pilots who know the jet from the outside, ma'am. When the new jets come, somebody who crewed the old ones ought to be up front.
It came out whole. The other answer she'd said once, in her own kitchen, and it had come out about the size of a seven year old. That one wasn't for the flight line.

Merritt let her finish. Then she nodded once. That's a good reason for the wing to want you, she said. It isn't what I asked. She went on to the next jet. Kit stayed under her own name a while, the wind going straight through her coat.

Sunday morning Boyd's door was open again. By then the whole ramp knew the colonel had stood at two two eight for six minutes. Nobody but Kit knew what she'd said there. She'd told the colonel it was with him and coming up through him. He didn't know that yet.

She was still reaching for the door when Boyd got up and shut it himself. The colonel stopped at the jet yesterday and asked where my package was. She told him what she'd said back, all of it. Boyd waited. Then she asked me why, and I gave her the wing. What'd she say? That it wasn't what she asked. Boyd looked at his inbox. Something moved in his face and didn't make it out.

Communication. When you've talked with someone's boss, you tell that someone yourself, first and in private. He shouldn't learn what his own airman told the colonel from the ramp. You also gave him the part that didn't go well, and that's what makes the rest believable.

At three on Sunday Boyd came across the shop to her toolbox with the routing slip in his hand. He laid it on the lid, took the pen out of his sleeve pocket, and signed the top block. Then he capped the pen and went back to his office. In eleven years he'd never handed her anything without a word to go with it.
A. BOYD, MSGT, in blue ink, pressed so hard it had come through on the back. She turned the page over and ran her thumb across the ridges.

He'd put his name on her toolbox. Under the shadow board foam in there, folded small, was the one piece of paper that could have told him he'd never owed her anything. She'd let him put his name right on top of it.

On the way out she stopped at the corkboard. Boyd built the drill schedules, and he'd already pinned up the next three weekends, March, April and May, a page each in his block printing. Every launch on every page had a crew chief's name beside it. Every one of them said DARROW.
Fisk read it over her shoulder. Guess that puts me on every launch too.

She couldn't tell what it was. A man keeping her close for as long as he had her, maybe. Or a man making sure the colonel saw her name on every sortie the wing flew before June. She stood there long enough for Fisk to give up and go get his coat.

Then she folded the slip in thirds and put it in her chest pocket. The work card from January was still in there, worn at the folds by now, with the five weeks on the back in her own handwriting. She slid the slip in behind it.
